strengths: Novel and well-motivated angle: the paper is, to the authors' knowledge (and apparently the reviewer's), the first to study coordination among value-maximizing auto-bidders under RoS constraints, complementing existing work on coordinating utility maximizers [9, 11, 29] and the largely individual-optimization auto-bidding literature.

Clean theoretical contribution with a necessary-and-sufficient characterization: Theorem 3.1 identifies Assumption 1 (Delta >= 0) as exactly the condition under which the highest-value-compete coordination mechanism reduces RoS violation for every coalition bidder, for any weakly overbidding algorithm; the negative direction is backed by an explicit trigger-style adversarial algorithm (Appendix A.2).

Results cover a broad and relevant algorithm class: Theorem 4.1 shows value improvement for any mirror-descent RoS auto-bidder without distributional assumptions, and the proof handles the subtle boundary case (Appendix B.2) and the degenerate case of no solution to G(lambda*) = 0, which is more careful than typical.

Theorem 4.2 gives an asymptotic optimality claim against all history-dependent coordination mechanisms, and the extension to non-i.i.d. valuations (Section 5) with a per-bidder condition (Assumption 2) shows where the i.i.d. analysis genuinely breaks and what weaker guarantee survives.

Experiments on synthetic distributions and the public iPinYou dataset are consistent with the theory across symmetric and asymmetric settings, with confidence intervals over 100 runs and a transparent performance summary (Table 1).

Honest limitations discussion: the authors clearly state that the non-i.i.d. individual-bidder guarantee is open, that the real-data model is constrained by unobserved bidder identities/valuations, and they list future directions (outside auto-bidders, other auction formats, private-value elicitation).
weaknesses: The model is quite stylized relative to the practical motivation in the introduction: values are i.i.d. (justified only by hand-waving that 'only similar bidders are chosen'), outside bids are i.i.d. from a fixed distribution, and the auction is second-price — whereas most large ad platforms have moved to first-price auctions, which the authors themselves note as future work. The gap between the motivating scenarios and the analyzed model weakens the practical significance claim.

The coordination mechanism requires a central planner to observe the realized values of all coalition bidders each round (Algorithm 2 computes argmax_i v_{i,t}), which is a strong informational assumption not clearly discussed as a limitation; alternative mechanisms without value visibility are deferred to future work.

The value results are only asymptotic (limits as T -> infinity, weak inequalities, no finite-T rates or regret-style bounds), so the paper cannot quantify how large T must be for the gains to materialize, despite the experiments using specific horizons (4000–20000 rounds).

Theorem 4.2's optimality result is somewhat degenerate: under Assumption 1 the coordinated multipliers converge to 0 so bids grow unboundedly, and the mechanism approaches the trivial upper bound E[v_(N)] of winning every auction with the highest-value member; this is an intuitively expected outcome rather than a surprising insight.

The real-world experiment design is quite artificial: bidder values are proxied by the empirical distribution of observed winning prices (winning prices are not valuations), the outside bid is drawn from the same pool scaled by U[1,2], and the i.i.d. resampling abstracts away exactly the advertiser/identity structure that motivates the paper. The real-data results therefore mainly re-confirm the synthetic findings under a different value distribution rather than validating the model 'under realistic market conditions' as claimed.
No code or artifact release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility of the experimental claims.

The paper studies and implicitly facilitates bidder collusion (a cartel mechanism that wins essentially all auctions under Assumption 1), which has clear anti-competitive and platform-revenue implications, yet contains no ethics statement or discussion of the legality/regulatory dimension; the discussion frames the findings as 'useful guidance for industrial practice' without addressing these concerns.

The necessity claim in Theorem 3.1 is relative to the existence of a somewhat contrived trigger algorithm; while technically valid, the practical interpretation of the Delta < 0 regime receives limited analysis (e.g., which realistic F, D pairs violate it, other than Assumption 1 holding for large N).

strengths: The paper addresses an underexplored angle in the auto-bidding literature: coordination among value-maximizing bidders (as opposed to the well-studied utility-maximizing setting), motivated by plausible scenarios such as third-party bidding agencies and multi-campaign advertisers.

The theoretical results are cleanly stated and appear correct. The necessary-and-sufficient condition (Assumption 1) for coordination to reduce RoS violation (Theorem 3.1) is a satisfying characterization, and the proofs (including the negative direction with an explicit constructed algorithm) are given in full in the appendix.

The analysis for mirror-descent auto-bidders (Theorems 4.1 and 4.2) is technically interesting: the reduction of the N-bidder coordinated scenario to a single-bidder problem with the maximum order statistic, the convergence of multipliers, and the boundary-case analysis in Appendix B.2 show genuine effort and care.

The paper is generally well organized, with the model, main results, proof sketches, and experiments clearly separated, and honest acknowledgment of limitations (e.g., non-i.i.d. individual guarantees remain open; real-data limitations are explicitly listed).
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to the classical auction-theory collusion literature. That a ring can raise members' welfare in second-price auctions by having only the highest-value member bid is a long-standing observation (e.g., Graham–Marshall, Mailath–Zemsky, cited by the authors themselves). The main new element is the online-learning/mirror-descent analysis, which, while competent, yields asymptotic (T → ∞) statements with weak inequalities (≥ 0) and no finite-time rates, leaving the practical magnitude of the advantage unclear.

Restriction to second-price auctions substantially weakens practical significance. Major ad platforms have moved to first-price auctions, and the authors themselves defer first-price/GSP analysis to future work. The paper's suggestions of 'industrial practice' guidance are therefore not well supported for the settings that matter most in practice today.

The 'real-world data' experiments are heavily idealized and arguably amount to a fifth synthetic experiment: values are drawn i.i.d. from a pooled empirical winning-price distribution, bidder identities are ignored, and the outside bid is an empirical draw multiplied by a random U[1,2] factor. The headline conclusion 'coordination outperforms independent bidding' is thus validated mostly in near-synthetic conditions chosen by the authors, with no comparison against any baseline coordination mechanism or adaptive outside bidders.

The central coordination protocol requires the coalition to observe all members' realized values each round and select the highest-value bidder — a strong informational assumption that is not realistic for third-party bidding agencies (which do not observe advertisers' private values per impression). The paper acknowledges alternative mechanisms only as future work.

Missing treatment of research ethics and societal implications. The paper analyzes and recommends a bid-coordination (collusion) mechanism among bidders, and its discussion explicitly frames the results as guidance for practice, yet there is no discussion of the antitrust/legal implications of bidder coordination in online advertising, nor of the welfare impact on the platform, outside bidders, or auction efficiency. The mechanism essentially redistributes surplus from the platform to the coalition via payment reduction; the abstract's framing of 'efficiencies' is potentially misleading.

Reproducibility is questionable: no code release is mentioned, and several experimental details (e.g., how confidence intervals are aggregated across bidders in Table 1, exact seed/simulation procedures for the iPinYou pipeline) are underspecified.

Some presentation issues: Figure 1 and Figure 2 are small and difficult to read; minor typos (e.g., 'seperately'); Table 1 mixes confidence intervals of very different sizes without discussion; and the theorem that coordinated mirror descent matches 'any coordination mechanism' (Theorem 4.2) holds only under Assumption 1 and asymptotically, which should be emphasized more prominently given how strong the claim sounds.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: coordination among value-maximizing auto-bidders under RoS constraints. Prior coordination work (e.g., Chen et al. 2023, Romano et al. 2022) studies utility maximizers, and the authors correctly argue that value maximizers behave differently (they overbid, and underbidding is trivially RoS-feasible), making the analysis distinct.

Theorems are well-structured and informative: Theorem 3.1 provides a necessary AND sufficient condition (Assumption 1) for coordination to reduce RoS violation for any overbidding algorithm, including a clean negative-direction construction in Appendix A.2 showing coordination can strictly hurt bidders when the assumption fails. This 'if and only if' characterization is stronger than a one-sided guarantee.

Theorem 4.1 holds for the broad class of mirror-descent RoS auto-bidders with no distributional assumptions beyond boundedness/continuity, and Theorem 4.2 establishes asymptotic optimality against ALL history-dependent coordination mechanisms (an upper bound of E[v(N)] is essentially best possible in a single-item auction), which is a satisfying and nontrivial result.

The proofs are careful and largely self-contained: the drift/potential-function analysis of mirror-descent dynamics (Appendix B.1), the boundary case lambda* = 0 (Appendix B.2), and the high-probability convergence argument for Theorem 4.2 (Lemma B.7/B.8) are all handled with reasonable rigor.

The paper is honest about the limits of its own results: the non-i.i.d. extension (Section 5) is correctly framed as a coalition-level result that does not guarantee per-bidder improvement, and the open problem of per-bidder guarantees is explicitly stated.

Experiments on synthetic distributions with varying N, T, and outside-bid distributions, plus the iPinYou dataset, are consistent with the theory, with confidence intervals reported over 100 runs and a clear aggregate summary (Table 1).
weaknesses: The model requires strong informational and structural assumptions that limit practical reach: (i) the coordination mechanism requires the coalition to observe ALL members' private values each round to select the highest-value bidder, which is a substantial informational requirement only briefly acknowledged in the discussion; (ii) results are for second-price auctions, whereas most modern ad exchanges use first-price or non-truthful auctions; (iii) values and outside bids are assumed i.i.d. across rounds, excluding auto-bidding outside competitors.

The value-comparison results (Theorems 4.1, 4.2) are purely asymptotic (T -> infinity) with no finite-horizon rates; by contrast, Theorem 3.1 gives a finite-T guarantee (T*Delta/N) plus a high-probability version. A finite-T version of the value results, even with weaker constants, would substantially strengthen the contribution.

The real-world experiment is weak as empirical validation: bidder values are simulated by resampling observed WINNING prices i.i.d. from a pooled empirical distribution, which conflates values with winning prices (selection bias: observed winning prices come only from auctions that were won) and discards the 2.5M records' temporal/identity structure. The outside bid is then scaled by an arbitrary U[1,2] factor. This setup largely re-instantiates the theoretical i.i.d. model rather than testing it on realistic market conditions.

The connection to prior work, while clearly delineated (utility vs. value maximizers), yields a contribution that is more an extension of Chen et al. [9] to a different objective than a fundamentally new technique; the coordination mechanism itself (highest-value bidder competes, others abstain) is the natural candidate and the analysis, though nontrivial, follows a fairly standard template (truthful-bidding benchmark + trigger-strategy construction + stochastic approximation drift analysis).

The paper does not engage with the regulatory/ethical dimension: bid coordination across distinct advertisers is precisely the conduct antitrust authorities classify as bid-rigging collusion. The benign framing (single advertiser with multiple campaigns, agency-managed portfolios) is plausible, but a paper demonstrating that coordination strictly dominates independent bidding and can even be asymptotically optimal should discuss detection implications and the risk of facilitating illegal collusion. This omission is notable given the paper cites empirical collusion-detection literature [12].

Presentation issues remain: typos ('seperately', 'coodination', 'monotonicaly'), some heavy notation (superscripts C,A,I,A), and there is no explicit limitations section; limitations are scattered across the discussion and Section 5.

There is a minor but noticeable gap between the theory (which permits ANY overbidding algorithm in Section 3, and mirror descent in Section 4) and the experiments (only one specific entropy mirror map is tested), so the empirical evidence does not probe the generality claimed by the theorems.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem: the paper appears to be the first to study coordination among value-maximizing auto-bidders (as opposed to utility maximizers), complementing prior work on collusive/coordinated bidding in auctions and on individual auto-bidding; the two motivating scenarios (third-party bidding agents, multi-campaign advertisers) are realistic.

Strong and clean theoretical contribution: Theorem 3.1 identifies a necessary and sufficient distributional condition (Assumption 1) under which coordination reduces RoS violation for every bidder, holding for any weakly overbidding algorithm; Theorem 4.1 proves unconditional total-value improvement for mirror-descent algorithms with no distributional assumptions; Theorem 4.2 establishes asymptotic optimality among all history-dependent coordination mechanisms under Assumption 1.

The proofs are careful and largely self-contained, including a nontrivial analysis of mirror-descent dynamics (occupation bounds via potential functions in Lemma B.2/B.3, a virtual-bidder reduction with clipped utilities, and a Lagrangian/dual-envelope argument in Lemma B.9), and the tightness of Theorem 3.1 is demonstrated with an explicit trigger-style algorithm in Appendix A.2.

Honest treatment of limitations: the paper clearly discusses the open problem of individual guarantees in the non-i.i.d. setting, the limitations of the iPinYou data (only winning prices observed, no bidder identities), and future directions such as first-price auctions and strategic outside bidders.

Experiments on both synthetic distributions and a public real-world dataset (iPinYou), with 100-run averages and confidence intervals, qualitatively support the theory and probe heterogeneous (non-i.i.d.) coalitions.
weaknesses: Model restrictions limit practical reach: results are for second-price auctions only (modern ad auctions are largely first-price), values and outside bids are i.i.d./static, and the coordination rule requires the planner to observe all coalition members' realized values each round — the paper acknowledges these but they substantially narrow applicability; the claimed 'practical robustness' in the abstract is stronger than the evidence.

Key value results are only asymptotic (T→∞) and rely on a horizon-dependent learning rate α=1/√T; no finite-time value guarantees are given, and no explicit convergence rates are stated for Theorems 4.1/4.2.

The asymptotic optimality result (Theorem 4.2) rests on multipliers converging to 0, i.e., the coalition bidding arbitrarily high; this is a somewhat degenerate optimum specific to second-price auctions with known values and says little about well-behaved finite-T coordination.

Incentive considerations are underexplored: the analysis assumes coalition members obediently bid 0 when instructed; while Theorem 3.1 shows individual utility (RoS) improves under Assumption 1, per-bidder value improvement is only shown empirically, and stability of the coalition (no profitable deviations, side payments, platform-side collusion-detection responses) is not analyzed.

The real-data experiment is essentially synthetic in disguise: values are i.i.d.-resampled from a pooled empirical distribution of winning prices and the outside bid is scaled by U[1,2], so it validates the theory under an imposed i.i.d. model rather than under realistic market dynamics.

Assumption 1 is a fairly strong market condition (the two largest coalition values must be competitive against the outside bid); the paper gives examples but does not quantify how often it plausibly holds in practice, and its failure case is only illustrated via a contrived algorithm.

Presentation issues: a broken reference '(?? 3)' in Theorem 5.2; a stray sentence 'See Appendix C.2 for the proof.' appears misplaced (after Table 1, at the start of the Experiments section); Table 1 appears before the section it belongs to; the Discussion is brief and does not discuss the platform/revenue or regulatory (anti-collusion) implications of coordinated bidding.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored angle in the auto-bidding literature: coordination among value-maximizing bidders (as opposed to the well-studied utility-maximizer case, e.g., Chen et al. [9] and Romano et al. [29]), and the positioning against prior collusion and auto-bidding work is reasonably thorough.

The characterization results are clean. Theorem 3.1 identifies a necessary and sufficient distributional condition (Assumption 1) for coordination to reduce RoS violation for every bidder, for any weakly overbidding algorithm; the negative direction (Appendix A.2) constructs an explicit trigger-style algorithm showing tightness. Theorem 4.1 proves unconditional asymptotic value improvement for mirror-descent bidders, and Theorem 4.2 gives an optimality claim among all history-dependent coordination mechanisms under Assumption 1.

The proofs in the appendices are substantive and mostly self-contained, using sensible techniques (occupancy/potential bounds for mirror-descent dynamics, a virtual single-bidder reduction with a Lagrangian envelope, Azuma concentration for multiplier drift).

The experimental section is honest about the limitations of the iPinYou data (only winning prices observed, no bidder identities, no coordination labels) and reports confidence intervals over 100 runs; the synthetic settings probe both symmetric and asymmetric coalitions, and the authors openly note that individual improvements are not guaranteed in the non-i.i.d. case.
weaknesses: The central mechanism has a severe informational assumption that undermines its practical significance: Algorithm 2 requires the coalition to observe all members' realized private values every round to select the argmax bidder. In the motivating scenarios (independent advertisers using a third-party agent, or an advertiser with multiple campaigns), private per-auction values are precisely what bidders do not share. This limitation is relegated to a single sentence in the Discussion rather than treated as a core modeling caveat, which weakens the paper's claim of 'practical robustness' and industrial relevance.

The main insights rest on well-understood properties of second-price auctions. Lemma 3.1 is immediate from DSIC, and the value results essentially follow from the observation that intra-coalition competition only raises payments while the max of values determines attainable value. The novelty relative to classic collusion results (e.g., Mailath–Zemsky, Graham–Marshall) and the recent value-vs-utility distinction is modest; the technical work is in the asymptotic mirror-descent dynamics rather than in the economic insight.

All value guarantees are purely asymptotic (limits as T→∞), with no finite-time rates, and the experimental gaps in total value are often small (e.g., 0.643 vs 0.666, 0.814 vs 0.819 in Table 1), so the practical bite of Theorems 4.1/4.2 is unclear. The real-data gains (0.620 vs 0.928) are driven by an artificial construction (outside bids rescaled by U[1,2] 'to maintain competitive pressure') rather than by the data itself.

The paper does not confront the welfare or ethical dimension of its subject. The proposed mechanism is, formally, bid rigging: it suppresses intra-coalition competition, which (as the authors' own results imply) reduces payments—i.e., hurts the seller/platform and potentially harms consumers. There is no discussion of antitrust implications, detection, or the distinction between legitimate portfolio campaign management and unlawful collusion, which is a notable omission for a paper explicitly advertising industrial guidance.

Several draft-quality and rigor issues: a broken cross-reference '(?? 3)' in Theorem 5.2; Lemma C.1's monotonicity claim substitutes a different competing-bid distribution without spelling out why this applies to the coordinated scenario where others bid zero; and the necessity claim in Theorem 3.1 hinges on an algorithm that conditionally bids the cap B, a somewhat contrived adversary for the 'necessary and sufficient' framing.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, the real-data pipeline involves several undocumented modeling choices (empirical i.i.d. resampling of values, bid scaling), and the i.i.d. value assumption itself is justified only by the assertion that 'only similar bidders are chosen to compete.'

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper is, to my knowledge, the first to study coordination among value-maximizing (RoS-constrained) auto-bidders, complementing prior work on utility maximizers (Chen et al. 2023, Romano et al. 2022) and filling a real gap in the auto-bidding literature.

Strong and clean theoretical contributions: Theorem 3.1 gives a necessary and sufficient distributional condition (Assumption 1) for coordination to reduce RoS violation for every bidder, valid for ANY overbidding algorithm — the iff characterization with an explicit matching construction (Appendix A.2) is a genuinely nice result, not just a sufficient condition.

Theorem 4.1 (coordination weakly improves total value for any mirror-descent algorithm, no distributional assumptions) and Theorem 4.2 (asymptotic optimality among ALL coordination mechanisms under Assumption 1) are significant. The proofs (single-bidder reduction, virtual-bidder argument, occupation bounds, dual envelope) are rigorous, self-contained, and technically sound as far as I could verify.
Results extend beyond the i.i.d. setting (Section 5), with honest identification of what is lost (no per-bidder guarantee) and an explicit open problem.

Experiments on both synthetic and real-world (iPinYou) data corroborate the theory, including asymmetric settings, with confidence intervals and 100-run averaging; limitations of the real data (only winning prices observed, no bidder identities) are transparently discussed.
Well written overall: model, algorithms, and proof sketches are easy to follow, and the related work carefully positions the paper against the collusion literature and auto-bidding literature.
weaknesses: Model realism gaps that limit practical reach: the analysis is confined to second-price auctions (industry has largely moved to first-price), stationary i.i.d. outside bids, and a central planner that observes all realized values to select the highest-value bidder. The informational requirement of value disclosure is acknowledged only obliquely in the Discussion (highest-bid-compete as an alternative); the theory does not cover it.

The main value results (Theorems 4.1, 4.2, 5.2) are asymptotic (T → ∞) with no finite-time convergence rates; the occupation-bound techniques suggest rates are obtainable, so their absence is a missed opportunity rather than a fundamental barrier.

The real-world experimental setup is quite artificial: bidder 'values' are resampled i.i.d. from a pool of winning prices, and the outside bid is scaled by a random U[1,2] factor chosen to 'maintain competitive pressure.' This makes the real-data results closer to a calibrated simulation than genuine empirical validation; no code or artifact is mentioned for reproducibility.

The necessity direction of Theorem 3.1 relies on a somewhat contrived trigger-style algorithm (bidding 1 after ever bidding 0), which weakens the practical meaning of 'coordination can hurt' — the negative result holds only for a specific algorithm class member rather than for the standard mirror-descent algorithms actually deployed.

Ethics/platform perspective is not discussed: the paper frames coordination as collaboration (agency-managed bidders, single-advertiser campaigns), but the same analysis characterizes conditions under which cartels improve welfare of colluding bidders at the expense of outside bidders and auction revenue; a brief treatment of the detection/mitigation implications (cf. Decarolis et al. [12]) would strengthen the contribution's responsibility framing.
Minor presentation issues: a broken reference '(?? 3)' in Theorem 5.2, duplicate equation numbering ('(6)' used twice in Appendix B), and duplicated lemmas (B.13/C.2) reduce polish.
